title: IOL Malposition: From Subluxation to Dislocation
summary: A comprehensive guide for the anterior segment surgeon on identifying, differentiating, and managing intraocular lens (IOL) instability, ranging from subtle tilt to complete crystalline lens or sulcus capsule complex failure.

Induced astigmatism, glare, edge glare, diplopia.

sections.title: Emergency Warning Signs
content: IOL touching corneal endothelium (risk of bullous keratopathy)
Pupillary block glaucoma
Retinal tear or detachment sign
IOL in AC causing secondary uveitis
Intractable IOP elevation

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Slit-Lamp: Assess tilt, decentration, and vitreous prolapse.
2. Gonioscopy: Evaluate zonular integrity and vitreous in AC.
3. Dilated Fundoscopy: Check for retinal breaks or vitreous pigment (Shafer's sign).
4. UBM/AS-OCT: Quantify IOL tilt and zonular dialysis extent.
5. B-Scan: Rule out retinal detachment if fundus view is obscured.

content.explanation: P: Pseudoexfoliation, Z: Zonular laxity, T: Trauma, C: Capsular/Zonular contraction

sections.title: Management Options
content: Observation (If stable, asymptomatic, non-toxic)
Medical (If IOP high: topical BB/prostaglandins)
IOL Repositioning (Scleral fixation/Iris claw)
IOL Exchange (If IOL damaged or lens type unsuitable)
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (Required for posterior dislocated lenses)
Scleral Fixation Sutured vs. Sutureless (Yamane Technique)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the contralateral eye for subclinical zonular weakness (e.g., subtle PXF).
Superior subluxation often points toward superior zonular dehiscence; investigate the inferior support before aggressive maneuvers.
If the IOL is dislocated into the vitreous, prioritize retinal health over quick IOL removal.
Modern Yamane technique is preferred for scleral fixation due to reduced risk of erosion compared to traditional McCannel sutures.
